summary: Specifies LISP-SEC, a set of security mechanisms giving origin authentication, integrity, and anti-replay protection to the mapping data returned in LISP lookups. It also lets a requester verify authorization for EID-prefix claims in Map-Reply messages. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When you ask the phone book for an address, you want to be sure the answer really came from the right place and was not changed. LISP-SEC adds that proof.

questions: how to secure lisp mapping lookups
how does lisp-sec protect map-reply messages
what is a one-time key in lisp
subtitle: Adds one-time keys and HMACs to LISP map lookups so a forged or overclaimed mapping gets caught.

tldr.problem: LISP looks up where an endpoint lives with Map-Request and Map-Reply messages. If a Map-Reply is not integrity protected, an attacker can change it to hijack traffic, impersonate an endpoint, or overclaim an EID-Prefix.
tldr.mechanism: For each Map-Request the ITR makes a fresh one-time key. The Map-Server uses it to sign the EID-Prefix it authorizes and derives a second key for the ETR, which signs the whole Map-Reply. The ITR checks both signatures.
tldr.outcome: The ITR gets origin authentication, integrity and anti-replay protection for mapping data, and can reject records for prefixes the Map-Server never authorized. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9303 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on the LISP specifications in RFC 9300 and RFC 9301.

sections.title: The Problem LISP-SEC Solves
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP, RFC 9300 and RFC 9301) splits addresses into Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) and Routing Locators (RLOCs). EID-to-RLOC mappings are found with a Map-Request/Map-Reply exchange.

If those Map-Reply messages travel without integrity protection, an adversary can manipulate them. The RFC lists hijacking a communication, impersonating the requested EID, and DoS or DDoS attacks. A malicious LISP entity can also overclaim an EID-Prefix and redirect traffic.

LISP-SEC adds origin authentication, integrity and anti-replay protection to the mapping data. It also lets the requester verify that the sender of a Map-Reply is entitled to the EID-Prefix it claims, according to what was registered at the Map-Server.
sections.eli5: Without protection, anyone on the road could swap the answer you got from the phone book for a wrong one. LISP-SEC makes the answer tamper-proof.

sections.title: Threat Model and Scope
sections.content:
LISP-SEC targets the control plane threats in RFC 7835 that attack EID-to-RLOC mappings: manipulating Map-Request and Map-Reply messages, and a malicious ETR overclaiming EID-Prefixes. An on-path attacker outside the Mapping System can, for example, hijack these messages and spoof a LISP node.

It makes two main assumptions. The Mapping System delivers a Map-Request to the intended destination ETR, and no on-path attack can be mounted inside the Mapping System. How the Mapping System is protected is out of scope. LISP-SEC also assumes Map-Servers can verify EID-Prefix authorization at registration time.

Map-Register and Map-Notify security, including who may register an EID-Prefix, is out of scope because RFC 9301 already protects those messages.
sections.eli5: LISP-SEC guards the trip of the question and answer. It trusts the phone company's own wiring, and it trusts that the book was filled in by the right people.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
Trust relationships between LISP entities are used to distribute a per-message One-Time Key (OTK). The flow is:

  • The ITR generates and stores an ITR-OTK for each Map-Request, and sends it, encrypted, inside the Encapsulated Control Message (ECM) to the Map-Resolver.
  • The Map-Resolver decrypts it if needed and forwards the request through the Mapping System to the right Map-Server.
  • The Map-Server finds the longest-match EID-Prefix covering the requested EID and adds it, with an HMAC computed using the ITR-OTK, to a new ECM. It also derives an MS-OTK from the ITR-OTK with a Key Derivation Function (KDF) and passes it to the ETR.
  • The ETR computes an HMAC over the whole Map-Reply using the MS-OTK, copies in the Map-Server's EID-Prefix authorization data, and sends the reply to the ITR.
  • The ITR uses its stored ITR-OTK to check the Map-Server's data, derives the MS-OTK itself, and checks the Map-Reply.

If the Map-Server is in proxy mode, the ETR is skipped and the Map-Server builds the Map-Reply itself.
sections.eli5: Each question gets a secret code word. The helper in the middle stamps the approved address list with it, and the final answerer stamps the whole answer with a second code word made from the first. Only the asker can check both stamps.

sections.title: Authentication Data in Messages
sections.content:
In a Map-Request, LISP-SEC data rides in the ECM, which has the S-bit set to 1 to show that Authentication Data (AD) is present. The ECM AD has two parts: the OTK-AD (the wrapped key plus its preamble) and the EID-AD (the authorized EID-Prefix records and an EID HMAC). The ECM AD Type is 1.

In a Map-Reply, the S-bit is also set to 1 and the AD carries the same EID-AD plus a PKT-AD: a PKT HMAC ID and a PKT HMAC that covers the whole Map-Reply, including the Authentication Data. The ITR sets the EID-AD Length to 4 bytes in its request because only the KDF ID field is present.

An ETR that supports LISP-SEC MUST set the S-bit in its Map-Register messages so the Map-Server knows it can handle protected requests. The E bit (ETR-Cant-Sign) is set only by a Map-Server, to tell the ITR that at least one authoritative ETR has not enabled LISP-SEC.

AUTH-HMAC-SHA-256-128 MUST be supported. Deployments SHOULD use it, except when talking to older implementations that only support AUTH-HMAC-SHA-1-96.
sections.eli5: Questions and answers carry little tags. One tag holds the secret code word in a locked box, one lists which addresses were approved, and one is a seal over the whole answer.

sections.title: Protecting the One-Time Key
sections.content:
The OTK must stay confidential and intact on two legs: ITR to Map-Resolver, and Map-Server to ETR. This can be done with DTLS or by encrypting the OTK with a pre-shared secret. The ITR/Map-Resolver secret MUST be independent from the Map-Server/ETR secret, to prevent ETR overclaiming attacks.

Implementations MUST support the OTK Wrapping ID AES-KEY-WRAP-128+HKDF-SHA256. A per-message key is computed as KDF( nonce + s + PSK[Key ID] ), where s is the string OTK-Key-Wrap. That key wraps the 128-bit OTK with AES Key Wrap from RFC 3394, using the initialization value 0xA6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6. The output is 192 bits: the top 64 go in the preamble field and the low 128 in the key field. A receiver MUST discard the message if the decrypted initialization value does not match.

Implementations MUST also support NULL-KEY-WRAP-128, which carries an unencrypted OTK with a zero preamble. It may be used only when DTLS protects the path. Otherwise the Map-Request MUST be dropped and a log action SHOULD be taken.
sections.eli5: The secret code word travels in a locked box. If there is no lock and no armored truck, the message is thrown away.

sections.title: Processing at Each Entity
sections.content:
A Map-Server decides what to do by checking the registrations of the authoritative ETRs, in order. If any registered with the P-bit set to 1, it answers with a protected proxy Map-Reply and sets the E bit to 0. Otherwise, if any registered with the S-bit set to 1, it forwards a protected Map-Request to one of them, and sets the E bit to 1 if some ETR registered with the S-bit at 0. If all registered with the S-bit at 0, it sends a protected Negative Map-Reply with the E bit set to 1. The Map-Server may change the KDF ID if it does not support the one the ITR suggested.

The ETR copies the EID-AD from the request and computes the PKT HMAC over the whole Map-Reply, keyed with the MS-OTK, with the HMAC field zeroed first.

The ITR MUST discard a Map-Reply that lacks the AD or fails either integrity check. It then discards the stored nonce and ITR-OTK pair. If the HMAC ID or KDF ID in the reply differs from what it asked for, it discards the reply and sends a new request with a different value, subject to rate limits.
sections.eli5: Each helper checks which of its friends know the secret-stamp trick and uses the best path. The asker throws away any answer with a wrong or missing stamp, then burns the code word.

sections.title: Validating Map-Reply Records
sections.content:
A Map-Reply record is valid only if both HMACs verify and the EID-Prefix in the record intersects at least one EID-Prefix in the EID-AD. The ITR then sets the record's prefix to that intersection and stores it in its map-cache. A record that fails MUST be discarded and a log action taken.

The RFC's example has a reply with 2001:db8:102::/48, 2001:db8:103::/48 and 2001:db8:200::/40, while the Map-Server authorized 2001:db8:103::/48 and 2001:db8:203::/48. Only the 103 record is usable. The /40 record is discarded because the ETR tried to overclaim it.
sections.eli5: Imagine a guest list signed by the host. If you claim a table that is not on the list, the doorman turns you away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The ITR-OTK MUST come from a properly seeded pseudo-random or strong random source. Shared keys should be provisioned through orchestration, refreshed periodically, and be unpredictable random values.

If the Map-Server and ETR are colocated, LISP-SEC gives no protection against overclaiming by that ETR, but it is inside the Map-Server's trust boundary, so the RFC leaves it out of the threat model.

Replayed Map-Replies are discarded because the nonce and ITR-OTK pair is deleted after the first valid reply. A replayed Map-Request costs the Map-Server, Map-Resolver and ETR a normal LISP-SEC computation, which gives the attacker a possible DoS but no other effect. DTLS SHOULD be used for message privacy unless the OTK is encrypted another way.
sections.eli5: Code words must be truly random. A copied old answer fails because the code word was already used up.

messages.label: ECM Map-Request + ITR-OTK
messages.note: ITR-OTK is generated per request and encrypted.

messages.label: ECM with EID-AD and MS-OTK
messages.note: EID-AD is HMACed with the ITR-OTK; MS-OTK is derived by a KDF.

messages.label: Map-Reply with EID-AD and PKT-AD
messages.note: PKT HMAC is keyed with the MS-OTK.

viz.caption: THE THREE PIECES OF AUTHENTICATION DATA

items.title: OTK-AD
items.text: Carries the wrapped One-Time Key inside the ECM.

items.title: EID-AD
items.text: Lists EID-Prefixes the Map-Server authorized, protected by an EID HMAC.

items.title: PKT-AD
items.text: Holds the PKT HMAC over the whole Map-Reply.

items.label: Some ETR has P-bit 1
items.desc: Send a protected proxy Map-Reply with the E bit at 0.

items.label: Some ETR has S-bit 1
items.desc: Forward a protected Map-Request; E bit is 1 if any ETR has S-bit 0.

items.label: All ETRs have S-bit 0
items.desc: Send a protected Negative Map-Reply with the E bit at 1.
